title: A relational theory of trust
authors: Eli Benjamin Israel
abstract: In this dissertation, I explore the nature of trust and how relationships are not only the environment where trust arises and flourishes, but more importantly, they provide its normative content. Relationships, I argue following Joseph Raz, are constituted by norms—ways in which we are committed to acting with each other as fellow participants. Trust, thus, implies a belief that our trustees will follow through with such norms, rather than aiming at particular actions. This framework grants participants agency in both shaping their relationships and determining appropriate actions within them, illuminating central aspects of trust's phenomenology, including its characteristic second-personal character. Each chapter of this dissertation focuses on a different puzzle in the trust literature, demonstrating the advantages of thinking of trust through a relational lens: In the first chapter, "Navigating Vagueness: Rule-Following and The Scope of Trust," I account for trustee discretion when explicitly defined expectations cannot be met. In the second chapter, "'I Trust You!' Sure, But With What? Understanding Broad Trust," I examine the phenomenon of broad trust—instances where we trust someone in open-ended ways that seem unconditional yet clearly have implicit terms and limits. Finally, in the third chapter, "Breaking Trust and Relocating Reactive Feelings," I aim to understand why trust violations typically represent not merely local practical failures but disregard for the relationship as a whole.

title: Talking with language models
authors: James Ravi Kirkpatrick; Alexandru Radulescu; Rachel Sterken
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce text that invites us to treat our interactions with them as conversations, and to treat them as intelligent interlocutors who remember, act, and make commitments. We argue that this conversational presupposition is mistaken. We introduce the artifactual stance, which describes human–AI interaction in terms of their design and affordances, rather than potential intentional attitudes. On our account, LLMs produce candidate text that users interpret, evaluate, and sometimes adopt as their own speech. We argue that such exchanges are not conversations, since generating text does not itself constitute an utterance or the performance of a speech act. Rather the communicative and normative work of interpretation, commitment, and action remains with the user. Our framework explains both the sophistication and usefulness of LLMs, and the conversational appearances that can be traced back to properties of the interface and to artifact design. It also reframes puzzles about AI reference, the persistence of supposed interlocutors, and responsibility for AI-generated text. These questions are better approached through an account of how artifacts mediate human linguistic practices than through assumptions about AI speakerhood.

title: Optimizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Privacy-Preserving Local Cognitive Agents Using Small Language Models
authors: Siddhant Parjane

title: Triboelectric E-Skin Patch Decoding Silent Speech for Advanced Human–Machine Interaction and Augmented Virtual Communication
authors: Ziwei Huo; Nuo Xu; Yixuan Fu; Rui Gu; Chao Liu; Zhong Lin Wang; Qijun Sun
abstract: Silent speech decoding (lip reading) represents an innovative hands-free communication method for individuals with laryngeal and lingual impairments, addressing critical daily communication challenges. Herein, a novel silent speech decoding system is proposed, which employs a self-powered, low-cost, and conformable triboelectric-based E‑skin patch and a well-trained multi-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) model. We systematically characterize the structural principles and electrical performance of the E-skin patch. A comparative analysis of labial kinematics during vocalized and silent speech is also conducted, which demonstrates strong consistency in time-frequency domain characteristics. The utilized CNN model is trained across 15 lexical categories (200 samples per category), achieving a high accuracy of 98.75% and demonstrating excellent recognition performance. Furthermore, by integrating human-machine interaction (HMI) and virtual reality (VR) technologies, we develop three representative applications, including a real-time lip language visualization system, an orofacial-controlled "Feeding Frenzy" interactive game, and a VR communication platform with avatar dialogue. This technology enables barrier-free communication for voiceless populations, demonstrating significant potential in HMI, augmentative communication systems, virtual reality integration, and biomedical rehabilitation.

title: Trustworthy machine learning of diffractograms to prevent silent failure of apparently accurate models
authors: Mohommad Redad Mehdi; Weiqi Yue; Ozan Dernek; Matthew A. Willard; Roger H. French; Frank Ernst
abstract: For automated analysis of diffractograms, it seems straight forward to use machine-learning models developed for images, which can indeed generate highly accurate predictions. However, the fundamental difference between images and diffractograms can introduce hidden vulnerabilities. As a case study, we analyze $$\upalpha$$- and $$\upbeta$$-phase fractions in Ti–6Al–4V using two independent synchrotron 2D X-ray diffractogram datasets. We analyze the performance of two neural networks: “IE,” pre-trained only on ImageNet (a database of natural images), and “ISE,” additionally trained on a large corpus of simulated X-ray diffractograms. Subsequently fine-tuned with just 250 experimental diffractograms, both models achieve similarly high predictive accuracy. However, robustness tests and attention mapping reveal fundamentally different internal logic. IE suffers from “surface-texture bias,” predicting phase fractions from irrelevant background and pixel noise. ISE, in contrast, evaluates physically relevant features – Bragg reflections – in the diffractograms. Accordingly, prediction accuracy alone does not validate machine-learning models. Trustworthy models for diffractogram analysis require physics-driven pre-training. Machine-learning models can accurately predict outcomes from diffractograms, but differences between images and diffractograms may introduce vulnerabilities. Here, the authors compare neural networks trained on natural images and simulated diffractograms, revealing that physics-driven pre-training enhances model robustness by focusing on relevant features, underscoring the need for domain-specific training in scientific applications.

title: A Brief Analysis of the Research Paradigm, Pathways, and Applications of Multimodality in Architecture
authors: Leilei Sun; Shiyin Li; Xing Zheng
abstract: The iterative development of data ecosystems and media environments in the Internet era is driving significant changes in the production methods and interaction models of architectural spaces. Multimodal theory, one of the hottest research topics in recent years, has seen substantial achievements across various fields both domestically and internationally. However, in architecture, the integration and application of multimodal research are still in their infancy, although showing rapid growth trends. Multimodal theory, which emphasizes using multiple modalities for information transmission and communication, can serve as a methodological tool for linking architectural spaces with human perception. Building on previous research, this article proposes a feasible framework for the application of multimodal theory in architecture, emphasizing the utilization of deep learning algorithms and software to recognize, extract, and integrate different modalities of spatial information (text, images, sound, and video), thus facilitating the creation of multimodal expressions of spatial experiences. Additionally, the paper discusses potential applications and future prospects of multimodality in architecture, including: (1) Interactive Space Construction through Multimodal Expression; (2) Multisensory Design with Multi-Subject Participation; and (3) Innovation in Urban Renewal Models Driven by Multimodal Media. Ultimately, the goal is to advance the integration of architectural design with modern technology, creating living spaces that are not only smarter but also more responsive to human needs, while also revolutionizing urban development strategies to optimize the built environment.

title: CART Rule-Guided Diffusion and AI-Synthesized User Preferences for New Media Art Generation
authors: Caixian Ye; Lijun Xu; Jun Tang

title: Cultural gene feature encoding-driven attention-based style transfer network for traditional patterns
authors: Tianle Tang
abstract: The cultural genes of traditional patterns are reflected in modeling units, constitutive order, color configuration and symbolic semantics. The hierarchical differences require that style transfer should take into account content structure, cultural attributes and target style. In order to convert the above hierarchical differences into computable constraints, this paper constructs a traditional pattern attention style transfer network driven by cultural gene feature encoding, which maps the features of the motif-element layer, the constituent layer and the semantic layer into a unified code, and establishes the correlation between the content region and the style region. The network controls the selective transfer of style features by dynamically adjusting the attention weight to complete the generation of target patterns. 3600 content patterns and 1200 target style images are used in the experiment. The results show that the SSIM of hierarchical weighted coding is 0.914, the recognition rate of cultural features is 93.6%, and the style similarity of four types of targets is more than 0.80. The constructed network can enhance the coordination of pattern structure maintenance, cultural semantic transmission and target style expression.

title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
authors: Gennady Andrienko; Natalia Andrienko; Manuel Resinas; Stef van den Elzen; Barbara Weber
abstract: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

title: SenseAlign: Understanding Vision and Touch through Language at Test Time
authors: Chuyang Ye; Qinting Jiang; Jingyan Jiang
abstract: Tactile-visual-language models combine vision and touch through a shared language space to recognize objects and materials. In real-world deployment, changes in lighting, contact quality or sensor hardware can shift visual or tactile inputs and degrade recognition performance. When both modalities contribute to a prediction, an unreliable modality can override correct evidence from the other. Since labeled data are generally unavailable during deployment, test-time adaptation offers a way to recover recognition performance from unlabeled observations. In this setting, we find that comparing accumulated observations with the text embeddings of candidate classes reveals modality reliability differences that confidence can miss. Refining features against competing classes also improves recognition beyond geometric alignment alone. These findings motivate SenseAlign, which uses a common semantic reference for test-time modality weighting and feature correction. Alignment Trust weights each modality according to its support for shared predicted classes. Anchor Realignment uses the same class text embeddings to fit a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from alternatives. Both modules use the same unlabeled history while keeping all encoders frozen. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate strong recognition performance under both natural shifts and controlled corruptions.

title: GAMF-Net: Grouped Availability-Aware Multimodal Fusion for Smartphone Skin Lesion Classification
authors: Yue Zhuo; Jingjia Yan; Fangyu Liu; Lingjun Liu; Zongjun Chen; Zhisheng Luo; Zhonghua Xie
abstract: Smartphone clinical images provide a low-cost data source for computer-aided skin lesion classification in resource-constrained settings, but images alone cannot fully capture patients' medical histories and lesion symptoms. To address the lack of structured organization among heterogeneous clinical variables, the ambiguity between observed and imputed values, and the risk that clinical information may interfere with visual evidence, we propose GAMF-Net, a grouped availability-aware multimodal fusion network. Ten clinical variables are divided into three semantic groups---demographics, history-related risk, and lesion presentation---and each group jointly encodes field values and field-level availability masks. The image branch produces the base classification logits, while each clinical group generates image-conditioned class-level residual evidence. Only available groups participate in availability-normalized equal-weight fusion; when all clinical information is unavailable, the model reduces exactly to the image-only pathway. We evaluate the method on PAD-UFES-20 under a patient-disjoint five-fold protocol with separate training, validation, and test partitions. GAMF-Net achieves an Accuracy of $74.17\pm2.85\%$, a balanced accuracy (BACC) of $70.11\pm2.11\%$, a Macro-F1 of $68.85\pm0.85\%$, and a Macro-AUROC of $93.42\pm1.20\%$, outperforming all image-only and multimodal baselines reimplemented under a unified protocol. Compared with the strongest baseline, MetaBlock, the corresponding improvements are 2.37, 2.59, 4.14, and 1.02 percentage points, respectively. Ablation results show that clinical information substantially improves class-balanced performance, constrained equal-weight fusion is more effective than dynamic fusion, and the lesion-presentation group provides the most informative clinical complement.

title: Assessing Representation Semantics Under Language Pretraining in Fine-Grained Classification
authors: Md Raisul Kibria; Sébastien Lafond
abstract: Understanding how supervision signals shape semantic visual representations remains challenging, particularly in fine-grained, low-data settings. Standard evaluations of vision models rely on downstream accuracy, which often fails to capture structural differences in learned representations. We propose a compact explainability-driven framework for comparing encoders trained with classification-only and caption-generation supervision on CUB-200. Using a controlled two-stage protocol in which both encoders are ultimately optimized for the same classification task, we enable a direct comparison of the resulting representations. Saliency maps are generated using attention rollout and gradient-weighted rollout and evaluated with five metrics covering faithfulness (positive and negative perturbation) and localization (keypoint emphasis, background attribution, and Earth Mover's Distance). Across random seeds and explanation methods, caption supervision yields representations that are more sensitive to the removal of salient regions, better aligned with annotated object parts, and less reliant on background regions, whereas classification supervision produces representations that are slightly more robust to the removal of low-saliency regions. An ablation study on the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset shows consistent trends across key metrics. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework makes supervision-induced representational differences observable and quantifiable beyond downstream accuracy alone. More broadly, it provides a systematic basis for assessing learned representations and comparing alternative training and transfer-learning strategies.

title: Decoupling Action from Egocentric Observation for World Simulation
authors: Yue Ma; Pengjie Song; Xinyu Wang; Yi He; Zeqian Long; Fangneng Zhan; Kaichen Zhou; Hongyu Liu; Hongfa Wang; Peihao Li; Haoyang Huang; Nan Duan; Qifeng Chen
abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.

title: Revealing Inter-Channel Modality Discriminability: Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network for Optical-SAR Object Detection
authors: Haojie Li; Yuanfei Huang; Lingfei Song; Jia Li; Lizhi Wang
abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and optical imagery provide complementary structural and appearance information for remote sensing object detection. However, substantial cross-modal discrepancies and indiscriminate channel interaction inevitably introduce redundant or conflicting features. Since different feature channels encode heterogeneous semantic information and contribute unequally to cross-modal fusion, selectively highlighting task-relevant channels while suppressing redundant ones is essential. To address this issue, we propose the Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network (CSIF-Net), which performs selective channel-level cross-modal interaction. CSIF-Net first employs a frequency decomposition module to construct frequency-aware SAR inputs, facilitating the separation of structural information from noise-related responses. It then models cross-modal channel relationships through a cross-attention channel selection module and dynamically partitions the features into shared and modality-specific components. Finally, a dual-branch fusion module performs cross-modal interaction and channel realignment for shared features while independently enhancing SAR-specific features, thereby exploiting complementary information and suppressing modality interference. Extensive experiments on the OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR datasets demonstrate that CSIF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in both horizontal and oriented object detection, surpassing the existing methods by 4.01% and 3.18% gains, respectively.

title: Timing-Aware and Interpretable Self-Attention for Event-Based Wearable Task Transition Detection
authors: Anda Ouyang; Siyuan Chen; Julien Epps
abstract: Task transition detection aims to identify when a person shifts from one task to another, providing a foundation for continuous health monitoring and timely context-aware interventions. While statistical and deep feature representations have demonstrated strong classification performance, they often rely on aggregated or latent features that are difficult to interpret in behavioural terms. Event-based features provide a compact and interpretable alternative by encoding behavioural and physiological patterns as discrete tokens with explicit semantic meaning, making them well suited for behavioural analysis in health informatics. Self-attention offers a mechanism for modelling interactions among such tokens; however, conventional self-attention classifiers primarily rely on token order and do not explicitly incorporate timing or duration information. As a result, informative temporal cues in event representations may not be fully exploited for task transition detection. This study proposes an event-based time-aware self-attention framework that represents behavioural signals as sequences of discrete events augmented with onset timestamps and durations. Event timing is encoded using a parameter-efficient kernel-based representation, while a novel type-aware duration embedding modulates information propagation according to event persistence. Experiments on a semi-naturalistic wearable dataset show that the proposed model outperforms existing event-based approaches, achieves performance beyond or comparable with statistical and deep-learning models with a more compact input representation, and provides improved interpretability through integrated-gradient-based analysis. These results indicate that explicit modelling of event timing and duration enhances both classification performance and interpretability, supporting reliable deployment in biomedical and health informatics applications.

title: Beyond the Prompt: Recovering Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models
authors: Zhengfeng Zheng; Minghong Fang
abstract: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.

title: AGR: Agentic Generative Retrieval with Tool-Augmented Search
authors: Ming Yang; Yaqi Yin; Zhibo Wang; Xiaoze Jiang; Jingwei Zhuo; Chao Zhang; Quanzhi Zhu; Weiguo Zheng; Liang Zeng; Yunfeng Zhao; Jiaqiang Liu; Kefeng Wang; Yupeng Huang; Kaiqiao Zhan; Xuanping Li
abstract: Large-scale search and recommendation systems derive much of their retrieval quality from rich, heterogeneous features, yet existing generative retrieval (GR) methods struggle to exploit such feature ecosystems efficiently. Static feature injection either encodes all available signals or places them according to predetermined schemes, increasing serving cost and introducing irrelevant or conflicting evidence. More fundamentally, existing methods cannot adaptively determine when a feature is needed, which feature to select, or where it should influence hierarchical Semantic ID (SID) generation. We propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), a tool-augmented paradigm that interleaves SID generation with on-demand feature acquisition. Conditioned on the request and decoded SID prefix, AGR decides whether to invoke a tool, which feature to acquire, and where its observation should influence subsequent decoding, thereby steering generation toward feature-consistent SID branches. To supervise this behavior, we construct tool-augmented trajectories based on feature applicability and information gain along the SID hierarchy, and train the model through SID pretraining followed by tool-augmented fine-tuning. Experiments on an industrial dataset and three public benchmarks, together with an online A/B test, consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of AGR.

title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Hayat; Jahangir Baig; Shayan Ahmed; Ahmed Faraz Ayubi
abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

title: Deep Learning-Powered Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis to Predict Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Response from Pre-Treatment Digital Pathology Slides
authors: R. Logeshwaran; Basheer Mohamed; Somnath B. Thigale; Balasubramaniyan Ramalingam; Venkatesan Kuppan; Mahalakshmi
abstract: Response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is governed in part by the spatial organization of the tumour microenvironment, yet most deep learning models applied to digital pathology treat tissue regions independently and therefore do not represent the neighbourhood interactions that shape immune activation. This study develops and retrospectively evaluates a Neighborhood-aware Masked Graph Spiking Neural Network (NAMG-SNN) that classifies ICI responders and non-responders from pre-treatment haematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images. Whole-slide images are stain-normalized, tiled and encoded into patch-level embeddings that combine statistical, textural, morphological and deep semantic descriptors. A spatial graph is then constructed over the retained patches and pruned by an adaptive similarity mask that suppresses weak or artefactual neighbourhood edges. The masked graph is propagated through a leaky integrate-and-fire spiking network whose accumulated firing rates form a spatial transcriptomic representation, which is finally classified into responder and non-responder categories. The model was evaluated on an integrated cohort assembled from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the Panoptic segmentation of nUclei and tissue in Melanoma pathology Challenge (PUMA challenge) and the Phoenix virtual spatial transcriptomics resource, using patient-level splitting. On the integrated test data the framework reached 97.31% accuracy, 96.94% precision, 97.82% recall, 97.38% F1-score and 98.87% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.947 and Cohen’s kappa of 0.946, exceeding convolutional, transformer and graph baselines trained under identical conditions. Transcriptomic reconstruction reached a Pearson correlation of 0.962, mean absolute error of 0.051, root mean square error of 0.081 and structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.966. Ablation confirmed that neighbourhood-aware graph construction, adaptive masking and spike-based learning each contributed to performance. These results are retrospective and computational.

title: Multimodal LLM-based Query Paraphrasing for Video Search
authors: Jiaxin Wu; Chong‐Wah Ngo; Wing-Kwong Chan; Sheng-hua Zhong; Xiong-Yong Wei; Qing Li
venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing Communications and Applications
abstract: Text-to-video retrieval answers user queries through searches based on concepts and embeddings. However, due to limitations in the size of the concept bank and the amount of training data, answering queries in the wild is not always effective because of the out-of-vocabulary problem. Furthermore, neither concept-based nor embedding-based search can perform reasoning to consolidate search results for complex queries that include logical and spatial constraints. To address these challenges, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to paraphrase queries using text-to-text (T2T), text-to-image (T2I), and image-to-text (I2T) transformations. These transformations rephrase abstract concepts into simpler terms to mitigate the out-of-vocabulary problem. Additionally, complex relationships within a query can be decomposed into simpler sub-queries, improving retrieval performance by effectively fusing the search results of these sub-queries. To mitigate the issue of LLM hallucination, this paper also proposes a novel consistency-based verification strategy to filter out factually incorrect paraphrased queries. Extensive experiments are conducted for ad-hoc video search and known-item search on the TRECVid datasets. We provide empirical insights into how traditionally difficult-to-answer queries can be effectively resolved through query paraphrasing.

title: Agentic code modernization
authors: Peter F. Peterson; Addi Malviya Thakur
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Software rots. Between refactors for new features, bug fixes, the continual march of cybersecurity advisories, and the slow drift of dependencies toward end-of-life, code must change or cease to exist. The simple act of keeping up can be overwhelming for research software engineers tasked with maintaining long-lived scientific codebases. To address this maintenance burden, the community has developed a vibrant ecosystem of language- and framework-specific tools, such as Dependabot for dependency bumps [1], Clang-Tidy for C++ static analysis [2], and Python Refurb for idiom modernization [3], alongside a host of similar utilities. These tools, while monumental in their contribution, are necessarily limited in scope: they encode a fixed catalog of transformations, they tend to operate on a single file or a single dependency at a time, and they presumably cannot reason about the broader architectural or semantic consequences of a change. More recently, agentic AI systems have arrived. Unlike single-shot code completion, agentic systems can read across a repository, run tests, observe failures, and iterate, and these behaviors, in principle, may enable a different class of modernization task. In this talk, we present concrete examples of modernizing Mantid [4], a more than 20-year-old C++ and Python project with roughly two million lines of code. We attempted to leverage agentic AI to perform maintenance work and modernization work on research software. Changes proposed by the agents were validated against the project's existing automated test suite and reviewed by human maintainers before merging. By exploring successes and failures, the presentation will improve attendees' understanding of when, and with what guardrails, to use AI to assist in modernizing their code. References Dependabot. title: An exploratory study of relationships between the executive functions and spatiotemporal control in a complex motor task: the spatial tapping task
authors: Mariama Dione; Gaëlle Alhaddad; Marieke Longcamp; Yvonne Delevoye
abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are cognitive processes enabling planning, control, and regulation of behavior. A variety of tasks have been developed to evaluate EFs, from complex reasoning to simpler inhibition tasks, reflecting the diversity of symptoms observed in patients with executive deficits. Recent research has emphasized their unity , proposing three core functions, working memory, inhibition, and switching, that share resources and combine to enable complex tasks. Yet, no single task captures both the unity and diversity of EFs, limiting the development of a unified framework and a balanced assessment. To address this gap, we designed the spatial tapping task, a timing paradigm combining finger tapping and circle drawing. Finger tapping requires working memory for explicit timing control, whereas circle drawing requires anticipatory control akin to switching to control movement trajectory, enabling implicit timing control. Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. A slow tempo favors discrete movements with long pauses between taps, whereas a fast tempo promotes continuous motion. Previous analyses supported a change in timing control mode with increasing tempo. Here, we explored the hypothesis that EFs are engaged accordingly: working memory in the slow/discrete phase, switching in the fast/continuous phase, and inhibition in the intermediate phase, where demands for continuous motion increase. In two studies combined into a single dataset, we compared scores with those from neuropsychological tests using correlations. We found that timing accuracy in the slow/discrete phase was associated with working memory, spatial accuracy in the fast/continuous phase with switching, and longer contact time in the intermediate phase with inhibition. We also explored whether performance was consistent with the EF deficits described in the literature, and the potential contribution of motor output, reporting scores obtained across populations with executive deficits (aging and dementia), combined executive and motor impairments (schizophrenia), and motor expertise (biscriptual writers), along with matched controls. Findings were consistent, although often more specific, and highlighted an important contribution of motor output. Altogether, our results provide initial evidence that the task can be used to investigate EFs, although cognitive, motor, and sensory contributions need to be disentangled to improve its specificity.

title: Enhancing synchronous patterned motion tracking and latency reduction through avatar prediction and visualization
authors: Adeyemi Opeyemi Ademola
venue: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: Enabling online virtual reality (VR) users to move naturally and contextually within their environment presents transformative possibilities for enhancing human motion prediction accuracy and fostering a deeper sense of connection in shared remote settings. Latency in motion tracking remains a significant challenge, as it directly impacts the user’s sense of presence and engagement in VR environments. This study investigates the integration of real-time human pose tracking and motion prediction techniques to reconstruct context-aware, skeleton-based motion sequences from historical data.The findings highlight that improved motion tracking and prediction significantly enhance immersion and social connectivity in VR, particularly in interactive scenarios such as online dancing. By leveraging historical motion sequences and machine learning models, this research develops methods to accurately render human motion in avatar or mesh formats, enabling seamless synchronization of movements with dynamic contexts, including music beats in paired dance scenarios. The integration of predictive modelling and advanced learning techniques offers a robust framework for creating realistic and engaging virtual interactions. This research contributes to advancing immersive user experiences in networked VR applications by providing a novel approach to tracking, reconstructing, and predicting human motions. The outcomes emphasize the potential of enhancing user connection, enjoyment, and realism in virtual environments, paving the way for enriched interactive applications in areas such as virtual performances, remote collaboration, and social VR experiences.

title: From utterances to actionable labels: Toward practical and scalable open intent discovery in production systems
authors: Grant Anderson
venue: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: This thesis presents novel contributions to the field of Open Intent Discovery (OID), addressing fundamental challenges in the unsupervised identification and labelling of user intents within unlabelled datasets. Existing work in OID often relies on small, static, and clean datasets, lacks robust methods for generating interpretable intent labels, and exhibits inconsistencies in evaluation methodologies. This research responds to these gaps by introducing a modular, fully unsupervised framework that supports the complete OID pipeline, from clustering to label generation, without requiring labelled data or large-scale pre-trained language models. A key academic contribution is the development of a fine-grained intent labelling technique based on an enhanced Action-Object extraction method. This method incorporates compound noun and adjective structures to improve the expressiveness and semantic precision of generated labels. The framework enables systematic comparison across different OID configurations, revealing how dataset properties such as utterance length, vocabulary diversity, and intent structure influence algorithm performance. Furthermore, a configuration prediction module is introduced to explore the feasibility of automating technique selection based on dataset features. Comprehensive experiments on both public and complex real-world datasets demonstrate the adaptability, robustness, and interpretability of the proposed methods. In doing so, the work contributes empirical evidence to support the claim that OID configurations must be data-aware rather than one-size-fits-all. It also exposes limitations in current evaluation strategies for label quality, underscoring the need for more nuanced, semantically grounded metrics. Collectively, the findings advance the theoretical understanding of unsupervised intent discovery and lay the foundation for future research in label generation, evaluation, and adaptive configuration in the broader field of natural language understanding.

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
authors: Neel Dey; Adrian V. Dalca
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. We use our 3D foundation model, anatomix, to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes and further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific, component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system placed first on the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at https://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
authors: Yang Luo; Tiantian Ji; Zifeng Kang; Yucheng Wang; Yong Liu; Zhiyi Yin; Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).

title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
authors: Zongsheng Li; Shengyuan Zhu; Zimo Zhang; Hanyao Li; Shengming Wang; Quanying Liu
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

title: More Interactions Make Communications More Efficient: A Directed Information Bottleneck Approach to Task-Oriented Communication
authors: Zhirun Zheng; Yiqin Deng; Phone Lin; Yuguang Fang
abstract: Task-oriented communication improves communication efficiency by transmitting semantic information required for downstream tasks, but may incur redundancy with previously transmitted information. To address this issue, we propose a variational directed information bottleneck joint source-channel coding (VDIB-JSCC) framework that transmits only previously unacquired information. Specifically, we use directed information to characterize the causal flow of task-relevant incremental information and theoretically demonstrate its advantages over mutual information and conditional mutual information. Based on this metric, we formulate a directed information bottleneck (DIB) objective that balances task-relevant information preservation and redundant information compression. We further derive a variational formulation, termed VDIB, whose tractable upper bound serves as the training loss. The encoder integrates a Vision Transformer for frame-wise semantic extraction and a Mamba-based causal state-space model for capturing temporal dependencies and extracting incremental information, while the decoder uses a Mamba-based state-space model for task inference. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 video streams demonstrate that VDIB-JSCC achieves higher classification accuracy with less transmitted information than state-of-the-art semantic communication methods. These results show that leveraging historical knowledge enables task completion with less information, improving communication efficiency.

title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
authors: Junming Liu; Marcel Böhme
abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.

title: Harnessing SPAD Noise: Test-Time Gated Attention for Indoor Depth Estimation
authors: Yiquan Gao
abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to hardware-dependent 3D sensing modalities, yet predicting precise metric depth remains a persistent challenge due to intrinsic scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and limited zero-shot generalization in unseen environments. Recent multi-modal approaches incorporate 1D/3D Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) data to resolve these ambiguities, but they mainly treat SPAD noise as a harmful artifact required for denoising or leave the noise ignored. In this paper, we present an essentially different insight: native SPAD noise is an informative prior that implicitly encodes deterministic environmental characteristics. Driven by this paradigm shift, we introduce a novel, lightweight Test-Time Gated Attention framework by Harnessing SPAD Noise, therefore dubbed HSN. Tailored for indoor scenarios, HSN leverages the synergistic combination of 1D SPAD histograms and Gate Adapters (GAs). Through three complementary optimization phases, it generates channel-wise gated attention vectors to dynamically adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, effectively resolving ambiguous scale and boundary challenges without the heavy computational overhead or dense 3D modalities that other TTA methods suffer from. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks show that HSN achieves state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in in-domain settings, while exhibiting even greater potential under zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, interpretability analysis reveals that the proposed gated attention mechanism adaptively shifts attention toward deeper semantic layers under intensifying SPAD noise. Code will be made publicly available.

title: MiDashengLM-Spatial: Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness
authors: Jinbo Hu; Hang Su; Lichun Fan; Heinrich Dinkel; Gang Li; Zhanchen Dai; Yiru Zhang; Chang Liu; Peng Wang; Junnan Wu; Jian Luan; Cong Zou; Heng Qu
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance in general audio understanding, yet most are designed for monaural input and discard the inter-channel cues essential for spatial perception. In contrast, existing spatial audio-language models are purpose-built for spatial tasks and fail to capitalize on the general understanding capabilities of monaural LALMs. We present MiDashengLM-Spatial, the first open-source end-to-end unified audio-language model, to our knowledge, which supports both general audio understanding and spatial awareness within a single architecture. It extends MiDashengLM with a spatial audio encoder, Spatial-Dasheng, integrated through a hierarchical semantic-to-spatial conditioning module that injects intermediate semantic representations into the spatial branch at multiple depths while preserving the original semantic pathway. To provide spatial audio-language supervision at scale, we develop a data synthesis pipeline that renders diverse spatial acoustic scenes with scene-level spatial descriptions and question-answer pairs. Experiments show that Spatial-Dasheng achieves strong performance on sound event localization and detection in real-world scenes, and that MiDashengLM-Spatial substantially outperforms existing LALMs on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Meanwhile, it remains competitive with state-of-the-art 8B-scale LALMs on diverse monaural benchmarks, demonstrating that spatial awareness can be acquired without compromising general audio understanding. The source code and model checkpoint are available at https://github.com/xiaomi-research/midashenglm-spatial and https://huggingface.co/mispeech/midashenglm-spatial.

title: Adaptive Semantic Communication with Residual Quantization for Resilient Vehicular Networks
authors: Xuanhao Luo; Ruichen Gao; Sandeep Sreenivasan; Zhizhen Li; Yuchen Liu
abstract: Vehicular networks require timely visual information exchange to support safety-critical applications such as cooperative perception and hazard awareness, yet transmitting high-dimensional camera data over bandwidth-limited and dynamic wireless links remains challenging. In this paper, we propose an adaptive semantic communication architecture for vehicular multicast that adjusts the amount of visual information transmitted according to current channel conditions, available communication resources, and latency requirements. Specifically, the visual encoder uses residual quantization to represent each image at multiple bitrate and reconstruction-quality levels. At runtime, the system selects an appropriate level based on the communication conditions, enabling it to trade visual fidelity for lower transmission overhead when network resources are limited. Context-adaptive entropy coding further compresses the quantized representations using offline-learned statistics, without requiring retraining for different channel conditions. This design allows the visual representation to be learned offline while the communication strategy is adapted online. Experimental results demonstrate competitive rate-distortion performance at ultra-low bitrates, improved delivery reliability and deadline satisfaction across diverse vehicular scenarios, and strong downstream perception performance, achieving up to 0.88 mAP50 while dynamically adapting to changing communication conditions.

title: TwinViT-DeepJSCC: Adversarially Robust Semantic Image Communication
authors: Maedeh Fallahreyhani; Paeiz Azmi; Nader Mokari; M. Reza Abedi; Melike Erol-Kantarci; Eduard A. Jorswieck
abstract: Learning-based semantic communication is vulnerable to adversarial perturbations introduced before semantic encoding or over wireless channels. This paper proposes TwinViT-DeepJSCC, a preventive-corrective semantic image transceiver operating under a fixed channel-use budget. Two Vision Transformer (ViT)-based deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) branches learn complementary latent representations protected by sensitivity-aware masking. At the receiver, confidence-aware fusion, blind corruption-severity estimation, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)-severity-conditioned denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) purification mitigate residual corruption without requiring attack metadata. Experiments on the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research 100-class (CIFAR-100) dataset consider fast gradient sign method (FGSM), projected gradient descent (PGD), natural evolution strategies (NES), and Carlini-Wagner (CW) source-domain attacks, as well as random jamming and channel-aware adversarial waveforms over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and block-flat Rayleigh fading. Under matched channel-use and attack budgets, TwinViT-DeepJSCC achieves maximum peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of approximately 9.5 dB under 20-step PGD and 10.8 dB under channel-aware waveform attacks over block-flat Rayleigh fading. Under PGD, it also improves Top-1 accuracy by up to approximately 38 percentage points over the undefended baseline and 13 percentage points over the strongest competing defense. Ablation results confirm the complementary contributions of the proposed transmitter- and receiver-side mechanisms.

title: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset
authors: Mohammad Abolnejadian; Matthew Brehmer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset 📄 Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3830398.3830522💻 Code: https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast Supplemental dataset for the paper: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings Mohammad Abolnejadian and Matthew Brehmer. Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '26). DOI: 10.1145/3830398.3830522 This dataset provides a collection of 43,878 open legislative records from the Canadian House of Commons, spanning 1994 to 2025, covering document types such as debates (Hansard), legislative bills, committee reports, petitions, recorded votes, order papers, and Library of Parliament research publications. It is released at three stages of the same pipeline: the raw collected documents, a processed corpus that has been passed through an ETL pipeline and chunked for use in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, and an embedded, pre-indexed vector store built from that processed corpus. The dataset supports the development and user study of the InsightToast project. The embedded form can be placed directly into the project's codebase, open sourced at https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast, where it serves as the knowledge base when InsightToast operates as a proactive side-channel assistant in policy discussion meetings. Usage in the InsightToast Backend Only qdrant_storage.tar.gz is required to run the backend. Extract it into the root of the InsightToast project, so that qdrant_storage/ sits alongside docker-compose.yml, and start the services: tar -xzf qdrant_storage.tar.gz -C /path/to/InsightToast/ cd /path/to/InsightToast docker compose up --build -d Contents File What it is Approx. size parliament_data.tar.gz Raw source corpus of 43,878 parliamentary records, as 57,124 files (.txt + .pdf) 8.1 GB compressed / 11 GB extracted parliament_data_processed.tar.gz Processed corpus: the same records cleaned, normalized, and chunked into RAG-ready JSON 2.1 GB compressed / 9.1 GB extracted qdrant_storage.tar.gz Pre-indexed Qdrant vector store, ready to mount as the knowledge base 21 GB compressed / 27 GB extracted parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the raw corpus, viewable without downloading the archive small parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the processed corpus small qdrant_storage.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the vector store small SHA256SUMS.txt SHA-256 checksums for the three archives small Verify the archives after download: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt Source Corpus: Raw Parliamentary Documents parliament_data.tar.gz contains open legislative documents collected across the range of record types produced by the Canadian House of Commons and the Library of Parliament, including the proceedings of debate, the texts of bills as tabled, the reports of standing committees, the petitions presented to the House, and the recorded outcomes of divisions. The documents were assembled from three public sources: the House of Commons (ourcommons.ca, including the Legislative Information service, LEGISinfo), the Library of Parliament of Canada (parl-gc.primo.exlibrisgroup.com), and the independent open-data mirror openparliament.ca. No private, personal, or access-restricted material is included; Member of Parliament profiles contain only information published in an official public capacity. Total: 43,878 parliamentary records, distributed across 57,124 files (43,634 .txt + 13,490 .pdf). Each record is provided as extracted plain text, with the source PDF alongside it under the same basename where one exists, so records that carry both formats account for two files. Temporal coverage: documents span the 35th through 45th Parliaments. Debates run from 1994-01-17 to 2025-10-10; coverage of the other record types varies by type. Languages: the source records are bilingual (English and French), as published by Parliament. Filename conventions: debates use sitting dates (YYYY-MM-DD- .txt); bills, journals, order papers, and votes use - - (for example, 37-1-C-10); petitions and Library of Parliament publications use slugified titles. Category Files Description debates/ 18,347 House of Commons debates (Hansard transcripts), one file per sitting day bills/ 10,561 Legislative bills, full text plus the original tabled PDF journals/ 7,038 Official Journals of the House (daily record of decisions) petitions/ 6,093 e-Petitions and paper petitions presented to the House votes/ 4,521 Recorded division and vote results order-papers/ 4,228 Order Paper and Notice Paper (daily agenda) library/ 2,202 Library of Parliament publications and tabled agreements committee-reports/ 1,577 Standing and joint committee reports, grouped into 27 committee subfolders politicians/ 1,319 Member of Parliament profiles research/ 1,210 Library of Parliament research and HillNotes publications committees/ 28 Committee mandate and description summaries Total 57,124 See parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt for the full breakdown, including all committee subfolders. Processed Corpus: Cleaned and Chunked Records parliament_data_processed.tar.gz contains the same corpus after the ETL pipeline that turns each document into retrievable units. Documents are parsed from their metadata header and routed by document_type. Bilingual records are language-identified with langdetect and reduced to their English content by an LLM pass. PDFs are structurally partitioned with unstructured's partition_pdf into text, table, and image elements; table elements are linearized into prose by an LLM, and salient figures are captioned, written to images/, and linked from their chunk via has_images. Records whose content is inherently tabular, namely recorded votes, petitions, and Member profiles, are rendered into natural-language narratives to keep them semantically retrievable rather than reducing to fields. Type-specific pre-segmentation then splits debates on speaker turns, preserving the speaker, section, and timestamp, before every stream passes through a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (1,000 characters, 200 overlap); each resulting chunk is tagged with its content_type (text, table, or image) and its provenance. The output is one JSON document per record, holding the record's metadata and its ordered list of chunks: { "metadata": { "document_type": "debate", "session": "35-1", "date": "1994-01-17", "language": "en", "source_file": "debates/1994-01-17-1.txt", "source_url": "...", "total_chunks": 51 }, "chunks": [ { "chunk_id": 0, "content": "...", "metadata": { "speaker": "...", "section": "...", "content_type": "text", "has_images": false } } ] } Volume: 42,014 JSON records and 2,170 extracted images, totaling 6,379,732 chunks, which is the set embedded into the knowledge base below. Traceability: every record's metadata.source_file links back to its file in the raw corpus. Coverage: most record types are processed in full; committee-report and library are present as subsets of the raw corpus. See parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt for per-category counts. Indexed Knowledge Base qdrant_storage.tar.gz contains the processed corpus above embedded and indexed into Qdrant, ready to serve as the retrieval backend with no further processing. title: A framework for digital twin integration into project delivery: Building on collaborative procurement principles in the built environment
authors: Corina Astrid Bagireanu
venue: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology has emerged as a potential enabler of systemic reform in the built environment industry, promising improved project delivery and long-term value creation. Yet, within a sector characterised by fragmented delivery models and adversarial procurement practices, DT integration remains limited and poorly defined. Policy direction remains underdeveloped, and governance support has diminished following the closure of initiatives such as the Centre for Digital Built Britain (CDBB), leaving a gap in national-level coordination at a critical moment for mainstream adoption. Despite rising industry interest and visibility among providers, and as the industry heads towards a more digitised, integrated future, there is a risk that DT may follow the path of earlier innovations: widely promoted but ultimately constrained by structural inertia and the absence of coherent implementation strategies. Fundamental questions persist around the distinction between DT and other digital tools, as well as how DT supports net-zero goals, and when and how it should be implemented. This study addresses these gaps by developing a novel Digital Twin–Collaborative Procurement (DT—CP) framework structured across the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) Plan of Work. The framework responds to the unique demands of DT implementation, introducing a preparatory Stage 0+ focused on organisational alignment, data governance, and long-term lifecycle planning. It also proposes a new classification model for DT to reflect stage-specific functionalities and support integration across the project timeline. The resulting framework is retrospectively applied to the Edinburgh Home Demonstrator (EHD) Programme to evaluate its practical relevance within public sector housing delivery, and provide an illustrative application of its stage by stage implementation. The findings demonstrate the interdependence between CP principles and the successful deployment of DT, revealing that DT adoption requires not only technical provisions but also, and especially, cultural and procedural alignment. The research establishes that DT value varies across project stages, and it is most effectively realised when embedded from the pre-design phase through structured interorganisational alignment. It further positions DT as a strategic enabler of net-zero objectives, contingent on the effective capture and use of data. This research contributes a practice-oriented model for DT implementation, with implications for governance and policy development, and encourages longer-term thinking across project delivery. Ultimately, it aims to demystify DT and bridge the gap between academic discourse and delivery, motivating broader adoption of DT as a catalyst for systemic change.

title: Evaluating data augmentation techniques in the classification of multi-station seismic-volcanic signals
authors: Franz Yupanqui Machaca; Pablo Salazar Reinoso; Claudio Meneses Villegas
